qs.q: A 32-year-old white male presents with a painless solid intratesticular mass. Serum tumour markers reveal a markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level, while beta-hCG is normal. Which histological subtype is most consistent with these findings?
qs.e: AFP is raised in yolk sac tumours and embryonal carcinoma, whereas it is never raised in pure seminoma. Choriocarcinoma typically elevates beta-hCG rather than AFP.
qs.s: Testicular Tumours, Hydrocele and Varicocele: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman is investigated for obstructive jaundice and weight loss. A tumour marker is checked which is elevated in over 70 to 80% of cases and is primarily used to monitor treatment response and recurrence rather than screening. Which marker is this?
qs.e: CA 19-9 is elevated in most pancreatic cancers and is used to monitor response and recurrence rather than screening due to false positives in benign biliary obstruction. Carcinoembryonic antigen is also raised but CA 19-9 is the primary marker for monitoring this malignancy.
qs.s: Pancreatic Head Cancer and Periampullary Tumours: Whipple Procedure: MCQs

qs.q: During routine follow-up evaluation of a patient treated for breast cancer, tumour markers such as CA 15-3 and CEA are ordered. What is their primary clinical utility?
o: Staging the axillary lymph nodes prior
qs.e: Tumour markers like CA 15-3 and CEA are used for follow-up and monitoring recurrence, not for initial diagnosis. Biopsy and imaging are required for primary diagnosis.
qs.s: Breast Lumps and Breast Cancer: Triple Assessment, Staging and: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with suspected malignant biliary obstruction is evaluated using serum tumour markers. Which of the following markers is most frequently associated with pancreatic and biliary tract cancers?
qs.e: CA 19-9 is the primary tumour marker utilized in the evaluation and monitoring of pancreatic and biliary cancers. Alpha-fetoprotein is primarily used for hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours.
qs.s: Surgical Jaundice: Obstructive Jaundice, Cholangitis and Biliary: MCQs

qs.q: A patient being evaluated for a suspected malignancy has a blood test showing elevated CA-125 levels. Which organ-specific cancer is this particular tumour marker classically associated with?
o: Ovarian cancer classically marked by CA-125
Breast cancer classically marked by CA 15-3
Pancreatic cancer classically marked by CA 19-9
Liver cancer classically marked by alpha-fetoprotein
qs.e: CA-125 is a tumour marker specifically indicated for ovarian cancer, whereas CA 15-3 is used for breast cancer and CA 19-9 for pancreatic cancer. Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in liver and yolk sac tumours.

qs.q: A patient diagnosed with metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma is monitored during treatment. Which serum tumour marker is classically associated with this malignancy and germ cell tumours?
qs.e: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is a classic serum tumour marker elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is typically associated with colorectal and gastric cancers.
qs.s: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Cell Cycle, Apoptosis & Angiogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: Which tumour marker is most widely used as a prognostic marker in lymphoma to reflect tumour burden and overall disease activity?
qs.e: Beta-2 microglobulin serves as the most widely used prognostic tumour marker in lymphoma. Alpha-fetoprotein is typically elevated in germ cell tumours and hepatocellular carcinoma rather than primary lymphomas.
qs.s: Acute Leukaemia (AML/ALL) & WBC Disorders: Haematology Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which tumour marker is monitored in pancreatic cancer, although it can also be elevated in benign conditions such as chronic pancreatitis and cholestasis?
qs.e: CA 19-9 is a tumour marker for pancreatic cancer that lacks specificity and can be elevated in cholestasis or chronic pancreatitis. CEA serves as a secondary tumour marker.

es.q: Discuss Ovarian Carcinoma under the following headings: Risk Factors and Pathogenesis, Classification and Morphology, Spread Pattern and Staging, and Clinical Features and Tumour Markers.
es.m:
- **Risk factors:** Nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause, family history, BRCA1/2 mutations, Lynch syndrome, infertility, endometriosis, and increasing age.
- **Protective factors:** OCP use, multiparity, breastfeeding, and tubal ligation.
- **Pathogenesis mechanisms:** Driven by "incessant ovulation" trauma, BRCA1/2 DNA repair defects, and two-pathway models (Type I low-grade via KRAS/BRAF vs Type II high-grade serous via TP53).
- **Surface epithelial tumours:** Comprise ~65-70% of all ovarian tumours and the majority of malignancies, including serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, and Brenner types.

es.q: Describe the types, clinical significance, and utility of tumour markers in testicular germ cell tumours.
es.m:
- **Diagnostic utility:** Tumour markers are crucial for both the initial diagnosis and for monitoring treatment response.
- **hCG elevation:** Always elevated in choriocarcinoma, and elevated in about 10% of seminomas and whenever syncytiotrophoblastic cells are present.
- **AFP elevation:** Elevated in up to 90% of yolk sac tumours and mixed tumours containing a yolk sac component.
- **LDH levels:** Serum levels correlate directly with overall tumour burden.
- **Pure tumour markers:** Pure forms of teratoma and embryonal carcinoma typically present with negative serum tumour markers.

es.q: Provide a comprehensive overview of testicular germ cell tumours, covering their epidemiology, key diagnostic tumour markers, detailed classification subtypes, and clinical management.
es.m:
- **Epidemiology**: Testicular tumours occur at a rate of approximately 6 per 100,000 males and are more common in white populations.
- **Genetic and congenital risk factors**: Brothers of affected males have an 8 to 10-fold increased risk, cryptorchidism increases the risk 3 to 5-fold, and intersex syndromes such as androgen insensitivity and gonadal dysgenesis also elevate risk.
- **Molecular hallmark**: The key molecular marker isochromosome i(12p) is found in virtually ALL germ cell tumours regardless of their histologic type.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Tumour markers are blood‑based proteins or hormones released by cancer cells or by the body in response to cancer. They aid diagnosis, staging, monitoring response and detecting recurrence, but are never used alone for screening.

sections.p: A tumour marker is a measurable substance, usually a protein, that is produced by malignant cells or by normal cells in reaction to a tumour. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical context, imaging and histology; markers support but do not replace tissue confirmation.
b: Serum assay (immuno‑assay) is the common method
Elevated levels must be interpreted with pre‑test probability

t.b: Is ovarian epithelial cancer likely? – Markedly raised (>35 U/mL) supports diagnosis, but can be raised in menstruation, endometriosis, pregnancy
Is a germ‑cell tumour or hepatocellular carcinoma present? – High AFP (>500 ng/mL) suggests yolk‑sac tumour or HCC; low levels do not exclude disease
Is choriocarcinoma or trophoblastic disease present? – Elevated β‑hCG (>100 IU/L) is diagnostic; normal levels rule out most trophoblastic tumours
Is colorectal or other adenocarcinoma present? – Rising CEA (>5 ng/mL) helps monitor known disease; normal CEA does not exclude early cancer

sections.p: Markers are incorporated into staging systems (e.g., FIGO for ovarian cancer uses CA‑125). Rising levels often indicate advanced stage or residual disease after surgery.
b: Stage I–IV correlates with increasing marker levels
Serial trends are more informative than a single value

sections.p: Most elevations are due to malignancy, but benign conditions are common, especially in low‑resource settings where infections and inflammatory diseases are prevalent.
b: Epithelial ovarian cancer → CA‑125
Hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk‑sac tumour → AFP
Choriocarcinoma, gestational trophoblastic disease → β‑hCG
Colorectal, pancreatic, gastric adenocarcinoma → CEA
Benign ovarian cysts, endometriosis, pelvic infection → CA‑125
Viral hepatitis, malaria, schistosomiasis → AFP elevation

sections.p: Patients often present with nonspecific symptoms (abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice). Tumour markers may be ordered after imaging suggests a mass or when a known cancer is being followed.
b: Unexplained ascites → consider CA‑125
Persistent jaundice with pancreatic mass → check CA‑19‑9/CEA

sections.p: Markers complement imaging and histology. Choose a test that answers a specific clinical question; if unavailable, rely on imaging and tissue biopsy.

t.b: Is pancreatic/biliary cancer likely? – High (>37 U/mL) supports diagnosis; normal does not exclude early disease
Is a germ‑cell tumour or lymphoma present? – Elevated LDH suggests high tumour burden or rapid cell turnover
Is a granulosa‑cell tumour suspected? – Raised inhibin B is specific; if assay unavailable, use ultrasound and histology

sections.p: Rapidly rising markers may signal tumour progression, metastasis, or treatment failure. Very high levels can cause paraneoplastic syndromes (e.g., hypercoagulability).
b: Doubling of CA‑125 within weeks → consider recurrence
Sudden AFP rise after resection → possible residual disease

sections.p: Treat the underlying tumour (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy). Marker trends guide response; supportive care includes managing paraneoplastic effects.
b: Surgery removes primary source, often normalising markers
Platinum‑based chemotherapy for ovarian cancer reduces CA‑125
Anti‑emetics and anticoagulation for paraneoplastic symptoms

sections.p: Serial measurement after treatment detects early recurrence. Lifestyle measures (smoking cessation, hepatitis B vaccination) lower risk of marker‑positive cancers.
b: CA‑125 every 3‑6 months for 2 years post‑ovarian cancer
AFP every 6 months after HCC treatment

sections.p: Benign conditions that raise the same markers can mimic cancer.
b: Endometriosis vs ovarian cancer (CA‑125)
Pregnancy vs choriocarcinoma (β‑hCG)
Acute hepatitis vs HCC (AFP)

sections.p: False‑positive and false‑negative results are common; always interpret in clinical context.
b: CA‑125 normal in early ovarian cancer
CEA normal in early colorectal cancer
AFP can be raised by liver regeneration after malaria

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with rising CA‑125 (possible tumour rupture)
Rapid increase in β‑hCG in a pregnant woman (possible trophoblastic disease)
New jaundice with high AFP (possible hepatocellular carcinoma)

faq.q: Can tumour markers be used for cancer screening?
faq.a: No, because of low specificity; they are used for monitoring known disease.

faq.q: What is the most useful marker for ovarian cancer?
faq.a: CA‑125, mainly for monitoring response and recurrence, not for initial screening.

faq.q: Why might AFP be high in a patient without cancer?
faq.a: Acute viral hepatitis, malaria, or liver regeneration can raise AFP transiently.
